name: Storm Chase
lines: Light damage: shingles and gutters torn off, branches broken, shallow-rooted trees pushed over.
Moderate damage: roofs badly stripped, mobile homes overturned, doors and windows broken.
Considerable damage: roofs torn off well-built houses, mobile homes destroyed, big trees snapped or uprooted, cars lifted off the ground.
Severe damage: whole storeys of well-built houses destroyed, big buildings badly damaged, trains overturned, trees debarked, heavy cars thrown.
Devastating damage: well-built houses levelled, cars thrown long distances, small missiles made of debris.
Incredible damage: strong frame houses swept clean off their foundations, steel-reinforced concrete badly damaged, high-rise buildings deformed.
Three or four cups on arms catch the wind and spin; the faster they turn, the stronger the wind. A vane beside it points into the wind for its direction.
Invented by Thomas Romney Robinson in Ireland in 1846. A sonic anemometer has no moving parts: it times sound pulses between its arms.
Air presses down on everything. An aneroid barometer has a sealed metal box that squeezes in when pressure rises and swells when it falls; a needle shows it.
Evangelista Torricelli made the first, with mercury, in 1643. Falling pressure often means a storm is coming; the centre of a strong tornado can be 100 millibars lower than the air round it.
How damp the air is (humidity) and its dew point
Two thermometers, one with a wet cloth on its bulb: water drying off the wet one cools it. The drier the air, the bigger the gap between them.
Storms feed on warm, damp air: on a tornado day on the Plains the dew point is often over 60 °F (16 °C).
How much rain fell
A funnel leads rain into a narrow tube marked in inches or millimetres; a tipping-bucket gauge counts each little bucket of rain as it tips.
The US record for one day is 42 inches (1,070 mm), at Alvin, Texas, in 1979 from Tropical Storm Claudette.
Weather balloon and radiosonde
Temperature, humidity, pressure and wind, from the ground to about 20 miles up

A balloon filled with hydrogen or helium carries a small box of sensors and a radio. It rises about 1,000 feet a minute and radios its readings down; the wind is worked out from how GPS sees it drift.
About 900 places in the world launch one twice a day at the same moment (00 and 12 UTC). The balloon swells as the air thins and bursts at about 100,000 feet; the box parachutes down.
Tornado probe (the 'turtle')
Pressure, temperature, humidity and wind inside a tornado
A heavy, low, cone-shaped case is set on the ground in front of a tornado so the wind flows over it instead of lifting it. Inside, sensors record many times a second.
On 24 June 2003 at Manchester, South Dakota, a probe recorded a pressure drop of 100 millibars as an F4 tornado passed right over it: the biggest ever measured.
Where rain and hail are, and how fast they move towards or away from the radar

The radar sends out pulses of microwaves; rain, hail and even dust send a little back. The echo's strength shows how much there is (reflectivity); the change in its frequency (the Doppler shift) shows its speed towards or away.
The US has about 160 big NEXRAD (WSR-88D) radars. Truck-mounted radars drive close to tornadoes: one measured winds of about 300 mph in the Bridge Creek-Moore tornado, Oklahoma, on 3 May 1999.
Where lightning strikes, and how far away
Each lightning flash sends out a burst of radio waves. Sensors far apart time when it arrives; the differences show where it struck.
Light travels almost at once but sound about a mile in five seconds: count from the flash to the thunder and divide by five for the miles (by three for kilometres).
How big the hailstones were and how many fell
A block of soft foam covered in foil is set out; every hailstone dents it, and the dents are measured afterwards.
The biggest hailstone measured in the US fell at Vivian, South Dakota, on 23 July 2010: 8 inches across, nearly 2 pounds.
Everything, while moving
A pickup with a weather station on the roof (wind, temperature, humidity, pressure), radar on a laptop, radios, a dash camera and a GPS that marks every reading.
Chasers look for the storm's updraft base and its 'inflow', and always keep an escape road open to the side, away from the storm's path.
How a thunderstorm grows
Warm, wet air rises like a hot-air balloon. As it rises it cools, and the water in it turns into cloud. If it keeps rising, the cloud grows tall and makes rain, hail, lightning and thunder.
The supercell: a storm that spins
A supercell is a giant thunderstorm whose rising air spins slowly, like a top. Most strong tornadoes come from supercells.
A tornado is a spinning column of air that touches both the cloud and the ground. Most are less than a few hundred metres wide, but they can be the strongest winds on Earth.
Rating a tornado: the EF scale
Nobody can measure most tornadoes' winds directly, so experts look at what they broke and work out how strong the wind must have been.
Seeing storms with radar
Radar sends out invisible waves that bounce off rain and hail. The computer turns the echoes into a coloured map: green for light rain, red and purple for heavy rain and hail.

A tornado WATCH means tornadoes could form: be ready. A tornado WARNING means one is happening or about to: take shelter now. Go to the lowest floor, in a small room with no windows, and cover your head.
Other storms and what they can do
Not every storm makes tornadoes. Some make giant hail, some blow straight-line winds, some lift whole walls of dust, and hurricanes are storms as big as whole states.

Lead forecaster at the Stormhaven Storm Prediction Office, twenty years at the radar. Explains watches and warnings, radar reflectivity and velocity, hook echoes and couplets, CAPE and wind shear. Calm under pressure; keeps a coffee mug that says 'It's not the heat, it's the humidity'.
Pull up a chair, the radar's busy today. See that hook on the south end of the cell? That's where I'm watching.
Professor Eli Brandt

Curator of the Storm Science Museum and a retired university meteorologist. Loves the history: Fujita's scale, the Tri-State Tornado of 1925, the El Reno tornado of 2013 (2.6 miles wide, the widest on record), the Vivian hailstone. Patient and funny with children.
Welcome! Mind the hailstone case, the big one's a cast of the real Vivian stone: eight inches across. Where shall we start?

Leads the Stormhaven chase team: drives the truck, deploys the probes, launches the balloons. Grew up on a wheat farm here. Strict about safety (never get in a tornado's path without an escape road, stay out of the hail core, never chase at night in the rain). Knows every instrument in the garage.
You riding with us today? Grab a vest. First rule: we always keep an escape road open.
Warning meteorologist, damage survey team

Weather Service meteorologist who leads damage surveys: walks the path after a tornado, matches damage indicators to the EF scale, measures the path's length and width. Owns the farm east of town with a storm cellar. Steady, kind, careful never to make light of people's losses.
This is where it crossed last spring. Look at each thing it broke and tell me what you think the wind was doing.
Cook and owner of the Twister Diner

Runs the Twister Diner on Main Street; has fed chasers for thirty years and heard every story. Knows the town's storm shelter drill by heart and the history of the town. Warm, teasing, generous with pie.
Sit down, hon, the pie's still warm. Chasers always come in hungry and leave with a story.
Fire chief and storm shelter warden

Fire chief of Stormhaven's volunteer fire department; sounds the outdoor warning sirens and runs the town storm shelter under the fire station. Teaches families their safety plan. Gruff, kind, a grandfather of six.
Siren tests are Wednesdays at noon. If you ever hear it any other time, you come down here, no questions.

From a pea (1/4 inch) to the biggest ever measured in the US: 8 inches across, 1.94 pounds, Vivian, South Dakota, 23 July 2010. Hail grows as the updraft throws it up through the freezing cloud again and again; cut one open and you can count its layers.
Read how hail grows
Updrafts carry raindrops above the freezing level; they freeze and are thrown up again and again, gaining a layer each time, until they are too heavy to hold up.

Deadliest US tornado: the Tri-State Tornado, 18 March 1925, Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. 695 people died; its path ran at least 174 miles. Widest: El Reno, Oklahoma, 31 May 2013: 2.6 miles wide. Fastest wind measured: about 300 mph, by a truck-mounted radar, Bridge Creek-Moore, Oklahoma, 3 May 1999. Most in one outbreak: 360 tornadoes, 25-28 April 2011.
